output.headline: UK and Caribbean agree to start reparations dialogue within a year
output.bodyHtml:
The UK has agreed to “structured dialogue” in the next year with Caribbean nations affected by the slave trade and its legacy, Commonwealth leaders have said.

Gaston Browne, Antigua and Barbuda’s prime minister, said there was a “consensus” in discussions between governments about a way forward on slavery reparations at the Commonwealth heads of government meeting (Chogm).

“There’s camaraderie and where we have issues that potentially could have divided us, we’re able to come to a consensus on the way forward,” he said.

Browne also praised UK prime minister Andy Burnham for being “very assertive in addressing [the] issue”.

“Perhaps there are some who believe that he may have dodged the issue as a relatively new prime minister. I think he has shown a significant amount of courage and goodwill, and I can tell you that he has developed a lot of goodwill with the Caribbean nations.

“And this structured dialogue that he has proposed, we are hoping that it will take place sometime within the next 12 months. We have also agreed in principle that by the end of this year, or early next year, that the whole framework for the dialogue would be established.”

Browne said the region would not be making “unreasonable demands on the United Kingdom”.

Burnham announced on Friday that he wanted to begin a structured dialogue and was open to Britain apologising, but ruled out reparations.

Instead, he proposed discussions on debt resets for smaller Commonwealth nations and announced £40m ($54m) for critical infrastructure in the Caribbean over the next three years.

A 10-point plan drawn up by the Caribbean Community’s reparations commission, which outlines the region’s vision for reparations, specifically asks for “debt cancellation” – not debt restructuring – and “monetary compensation”, arguing that former colonies’ “existing debts are intergenerational and are ultimately and intimately tied to centuries of colonial extraction”.

Asked whether Caribbean nations would urge Burnham to approach the talks with an open mind on reparations, Browne said: “We see the prime minister as an open-minded person, and the issue certainly will be raised.

“On the commencement of the structured dialogue, he has taken his position and we are very clear on our position that reparations are important, that reparations must be part of this structured dialogue and we remain very optimistic that we will come to a consensus on the issue.”

Leading figures in the Caribbean reparatory justice movement have said that debt relief and development assistance from the UK cannot be a replacement for reparations for centuries of slavery.

Ralph Gonsalves, a former prime minister of St Vincent and the Grenadines and a senior figure in the reparatory justice movement’s Repair Campaign, said: “When I listened to Andy Burnham, and I listened to the king, and they’re talking about what is helpful is not reparations, but for them to work on specific things like debt relief, and education and health, and climate change infrastructure.

“Now, all those things are within the 10-point plan. But they are also within the sustainable development goals of 2015, which we all signed on to at the United Nations,” he told the Guardian.

He added: “There are things in the reparatory justice 10-point plan which deal with issues … the first one is the ecology, and then psychological repair. And for people like members of the Rastafari faith, or brothers and sisters who may wish repatriation, that’s something we have to work out with African countries, those who want to go back. But there are financial implications in that. So you’ll have to have a separate carve-out on the basis of the 10-point plan.”

Labour MP Bell Ribeiro-Addy, chair of the House of Commons’ all-party parliamentary group for Afrikan Reparations, said the question was fundamentally about “agency”.

Speaking at an event on Tuesday to launch a “global reparations caravan”, which will travel across countries to educate and engage people in the reparations movement, she said: “So when it comes now to reparative justice, and as we move forward in the movement, I have to be clear with everybody, it has to be about agency, not making deals here and there, because agency was the crime. When you think about what was taken from people of African descent when they were enslaved, it was their agency, their right to decide all of these different things about their lives.

“So when reparative justice arrangements are being made, it absolutely has to be made with those who were affected, because if it is done to us, it is not reparations. I don’t know what it is, but it is not reparative justice.”

Gonsalves said the danger of reducing reparatory justice to development assistance was that such assistance remained discretionary on the UK’s part. “We have to understand the specificities of reparatory justice as distinct from general sustainable development goals. They’re shaping the discussion only within the frame of sustainable development goals,” he said.

Related: King Charles addresses summit as demands for slavery apology grow

Prof Kingsley Abbott, a human rights lawyer and director of the Institute of Commonwealth Studies at the University of London, also stressed the importance of harmed communities having a decisive say in what reparations should entail.

Speaking at the global reparations caravan launch on Tuesday, he said: “It’s for you to say. It’s your story. It’s your lived experience. But it’s time to start listening to those who continue to suffer from those crimes even today. It’s time to listen to you and to listen and learn from you.

“I reflected on my work as a human rights lawyer in different parts of the world. And in that time, I’ve met with many different victims of serious human rights violations, atrocity crimes, and their families and their descendants in places like Guatemala, Colombia, Nepal, Myanmar. And here in Antigua tonight, I’m meeting with all of you.

“Wherever those victims of those terrible crimes and their families were from, and whatever their faith, whatever their ethnicity, whatever their beliefs, they all had one thing in common. When I met with them, they all said that they wanted justice. And they wanted not only justice, but they wanted to be made whole again.”

A spokesperson for the Foreign Office said: “The prime minister wants to build stronger relationships to renew the relevance of the Commonwealth in a new era. We will do that by facing our past together and focusing on a future where every person living within it has equality, security and hope.

“We are already committed to working with Commonwealth partners on issues facing the world, including the role of private finance in tackling global debt issues, addressing the climate crisis, and supporting economic development. We will continue to do so.”
output.standfirst: Antigua and Barbuda’s prime minister Gaston Browne hails a ‘consensus’ at the Commonwealth summit, as the UK rules out reparations but commits to debt talks and £40m in Caribbean infrastructure funding
output.progress: The UK and Caribbean nations have agreed a timeline for formal talks, with Andy Burnham pledging £40m for Caribbean infrastructure and debt-relief discussions.

output.headline: Joshua Wong sentenced to 10 years in Hong Kong national security case
output.bodyHtml:
Hong Kong activist Joshua Wong has been sentenced to 10 years in prison after earlier pleading guilty to “foreign collusion”, his second conviction under a national security law that critics say has been used to silence political opposition in the city.

Wong, who rose to prominence as the teenage face of Hong Kong’s 2014 pro-democracy demonstrations, submitted his guilty plea in September. He had been accused of working with the exiled Hong Kong activist Nathan Law to urge foreign powers to impose sanctions, blockades or other hostile measures against China.

In his ruling on Thursday, high ​court Judge William Tam ‌described Wong’s actions as “grave in nature”.

He said Wong had visited the US to seek foreign interference ahead of the national security law’s introduction in 2020, and continued to share posts on social media by Law calling for sanctions after it was enacted.

Wong’s role was to “supply his underground support” and “arouse the attention of foreign countries to bolster the cause”, the judge said. He described Wong’s actions as part of a “scheme” to collude with foreign governments.

Tam said Wong’s sentence would run concurrently with the remaining term of his previous national security offence.

After the ruling, Law said in a statement: “It’s incredibly sad to see my friend Joshua Wong suffer another sentencing over his peaceful advocacy work for Hong Kong’s democracy.

“The signal the sentencing sent to the world is that [China] is determined to quash any hopes for freedom and democracy on its soil.”

Amnesty International’s deputy regional director, Sarah Brooks, said: “Today’s sentence is another grim reminder of how Hong Kong’s national security law has become a tool to punish dissent rather than to genuinely protect national security.”

Wong wore a dark blue shirt and thick rimmed spectacles in court, and nodded and bowed as supporters waved. Dozens of people had waited in line outside the court building for the hearing, amid a heavy police presence. A group of international diplomats were also present for the sentencing.

The former student leader is already serving a prison term of four years and eight months – imposed in November 2024 – for conspiracy to commit subversion for his role in an unofficial primary election. He has spent nearly six years in detention and had been due to be released in January 2027.

Related: ‘Hong Kong is at a crossroads’: inside prison with the student who took on Beijing

Wong, 30, gained international attention during the 2014 Umbrella protests, which paralysed the city’s financial centre and galvanised a generation of young people. In October 2014, he appeared on the cover of a Time magazine under the headline: “The Face of Protest”.

When protests erupted in 2019 over a proposed extradition bill, Wong was serving a prison sentence for his role in the 2014 demonstrations. He was released at the height of the protests and immediately took to the streets.

The following year, Beijing introduced a sweeping national security law it said was needed to restore stability to the former British colony, but critics say has been used to target political opposition, dissolve civil society groups and silence independent media.

Wong is the only activist in Hong Kong prosecuted twice under the law and his sentencing on Thursday was criticised by human rights groups and supporters.
output.standfirst: The pro-democracy activist, 30, has been detained since 2020 and is the only person in Hong Kong prosecuted twice under the national security law

output.headline: Treatment charities call for new UK drugs strategy to save lives
output.bodyHtml:
The government “must act now to reverse this deadly trend”, charities have said, after cocaine overtook heroin as the biggest cause of drug deaths in England and Wales, figures from the Office for National Statistics show, with 1,233 deaths caused by cocaine last year.

Drug deaths fell slightly in 2025 compared with the previous year, though they “remained historically high” at double the rates of 10 years ago, with cocaine-specific deaths four times higher than a decade ago and eight times higher than in 2010.

The Guardian revealed last week that police were recording a growing number of crimes linked to cocaine, including assaults, domestic abuse and dangerous driving.

Related: Ageing users and record deaths – the data behind Britain’s multibillion-pound cocaine habit

Wastewater analysis shows consumption of the class A drug is surging, becoming a more common sight in pubs, festivals and workplaces. It is linked with a rise of 10% in crime associated with cocaine since 2019.

For the first time, cocaine was the drug most involved in drug-related deaths, the figures show, amounting to 22%. This included its use as a powder and deaths caused by injecting the drug or smoking it as crack cocaine.

A total of 64% of cocaine deaths registered were of people over the age of 40, a trend also seen among people seeking help from drug treatment services.

Overall, 5,519 deaths related to drug poisoning were registered last year, 46 fewer than in 2024.

The north-east of England had the highest rates of drug deaths, at 135.2 deaths per million people in 2025, while London had the lowest rate at 58.3 deaths per million. Deaths were five times higher in the most deprived areas than the least deprived.

The statistics also showed rates of deaths from ketamine had risen dramatically from a very low base a decade ago. Ketamine was mentioned in 115 deaths in 2025, compared with 27 in 2020 and seven in 2015.

Niamh Eastwood, the executive director of Release, the UK’s national centre of expertise on drugs and drug laws, said cocaine deaths were “a direct result of policy failures both in the UK and internationally”.

She said: “Cocaine production is at an all-time high; it’s more available, cheaper and purer than ever, despite billions spent on trying to disrupt or eradicate the trade.”

The NGO said the UK’s focus on punishing drug use prevented drug services offering harm-reduction interventions, “meaning there is literally nothing practical on offer for people who use [cocaine]”.

Mike Trace, the chief executive of the social justice charity Forward Trust, said the overall drug-related death rate was “a national scandal” that needed urgent attention.

He said: “That cocaine has risen to the top of the statistics for drug-related deaths should come as no surprise. We’re facing the perfect storm of record levels of production in South America leading to falling prices combined with increasing purity, which means increasing potency and risk.”

Will Haydock, the chief executive of Collective Voice, a drug treatment campaigning charity, said that improvements previously made were “now at risk due to government inaction”.

Related: ‘He was like 10 men after taking cocaine‘: how Britain’s drug habit is fuelling domestic abuse

“For over two years the government has been largely silent on addiction, and has paused the planned investment programme, freezing funding at year-three levels rather than continuing to follow the path laid out by the independent review of drugs, which has amounted to a real-terms cut at a time when we are trying to support more people in treatment than ever before,” he said.

The independent review led by Prof Carol Black was commissioned by Boris Johnson’s government and published in 2021, and recommended an overhaul of drug treatment services.

Haydock said: “If the current prime minister is to achieve his ambitions on a whole range of policy issues – including violence against women and girls, the crisis in the criminal justice system, homelessness, and young people’s employment and mental health – then we must talk about drugs, and specifically treatment and recovery services.

“We urgently need a new drugs strategy with clear priorities, including reducing drug-related deaths. If we get our response to alcohol and other drugs right, we can save and improve hundreds of thousands of lives.”
output.standfirst: Charities are calling on ministers for a new national drugs strategy, after cocaine overtook heroin as the leading cause of drug deaths in England and Wales, with cocaine deaths eight times higher than in 2010
output.progress: Addiction charities are urging ministers to publish a new drugs strategy with clear priorities for cutting drug-related deaths.

output.headline: British healthcare worker who helped fight Ebola evacuated home for care
output.bodyHtml:
A British healthcare worker with Ebola is being evacuated from the Democratic Republic of the Congo to the UK for medical treatment, it has been confirmed.

“A British citizen currently in the DR Congo has tested positive for Ebola,” a spokesperson for the UK government said in a statement on Wednesday. “The UK has well-established procedures for dealing with cases like this, and those processes have been activated … The risk to the UK public from Ebola remains low.”

The patient, whose identity is unknown, is in a stable condition and is expected to arrive in the UK on Wednesday or Thursday before being transferred in a specialist ambulance to a “high consequence” infectious disease unit, according to an official document seen by Reuters.

A humanitarian organisation sent the worker to DR Congo to help in the response to the outbreak, which is the second largest on record. It is the first case involving a British national contracting Ebola in the current outbreak.

The Royal Free hospital in London has a high-level isolation unit for infectious diseases such as Ebola; other centres are in Newcastle and Liverpool.

Ebola is a highly contagious, severe and often fatal illness. It is spread through direct contact with body fluids such as the blood or vomit of infected people, or dead bodies.

Vaccine trials for the Bundibugyo virus behind the outbreak are under way, though it has no approved treatment yet. The current outbreak, declared on 15 May by DR Congo’s health ministry, has surpassed 10,000 cases, and 5,000 deaths, and is the 17th in DR Congo since Ebola was identified, making it the largest and deadliest in the country’s history.

Since the outbreak started, it has spread to Kenya and Uganda in east Africa, while last month Nigeria confirmed a case in the capital, Abuja, after a woman who arrived from Uganda tested positive for the virus. She, along with a close contact, were evacuated to Switzerland for treatment.

In an interview with the Guardian last month, Dr Jean Kaseya, the director general of the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), said the “unprecedented” spread of the Ebola outbreak meant it could reach the UK and other countries.

“We want all countries to know that they are not safe if they don’t take appropriate measures,” he said. “Each country, not only in the African region, but all continents, must now increase the preparedness level and the possibility for treatment.

“It is the first time three African regions have been affected [by Ebola]. The geographic extension of this outbreak is unprecedented.”

Other patients have already been successfully medically evacuated for specialised care since the start of the outbreak, including two sent to Germany and one to the Netherlands. Another case was reported in France in July.

British health authorities say the risk ⁠to the wider public from imported Ebola cases remains low and the NHS has procedures in place to manage suspected and confirmed infections.

There have only been four confirmed cases recorded in Britain since 1976, ‌according to the UK Health Security Agency.
output.standfirst: The British citizen, sent to DR Congo to help tackle an Ebola outbreak that has infected more than 10,000 people and killed 5,000, is in a stable condition and being flown home to a specialist unit
output.progress: UK health authorities have activated well-established evacuation and treatment procedures, and say the risk to the public remains low.

output.headline: Nine men on trial in Manchester over abuse of Stockport woman
output.bodyHtml:
A husband who invited other men to rape and sexually assault his wife arranged for “more and more individuals” to visit his marital home as he resolved “to satisfy his own perversity”, a jury has been told.

The husband, who is in his 60s and from Stockport in Greater Manchester, has pleaded guilty to more than 60 offences against his wife. He cannot be named in order to protect the anonymity of his victim.

Nine men are on trial at Manchester Minshull Street crown court accused of either taking part in the abuse of the victim, or encouraging the offending online while “hiding behind the screens of their mobile telephones and computers”.

One of the “non-contact” alleged offenders, Daniel Rayner, 42, of Whitstable, Kent, repeatedly sought imagery of the abuse of the victim, the court heard. He told the husband: “Passed out ones are obviously better,” and: “Hope she’s being used tonight.”

The husband had shared imagery of other men, Graham Brougham and Sean Peers, assaulting his wife, and when Rayner asked: “So I guessing she had no idea he had stripped and fucked her,” the husband confirmed she did not.

Rayner then asked him: “What did you give her … I’ve always used GHB.”

Rayner denies conspiracy to rape, conspiracy to assault by penetration and conspiracy to administer a substance with intent.

Setting out a timeline of the allegations, the prosecutor Louise Oakley KC told the court that by the start of January 2025: “[The husband] doesn’t appear to have had any new year’s resolutions to stop his offending on his wife.”

“If anything, his resolve to satisfy his own perversity continued,” she said. “With arrangements being made for more and more individuals to attend.”

Two of the defendants, Philip Wild, 59, and Mohammed Sabir, 28, both from Stockport, had sexually abused the woman one after the other in a single night in early 2025, the court heard.

Oakley said Wild was “fully aware” that the woman was not conscious and not able to consent to any sexual activity. “He’d been there before so that was no surprise, and certainly was no deterrent the state he’d seen her in before,” she told the court.

Wild has pleaded not guilty to sexual assault, attempted rape, assault by penetration and conspiracy to rape.

Oakley told the court that Sabir also “knew before he went into the bedroom” that the victim was not conscious, and “at no point” did he attempt to communicate with her, or seek her consent.

The husband later asked him to write a review on a swingers website, the court heard, and the jury was shown the review, which read: “Really easy to set up a meet. It was my first [experience] fucking someone’s wife in front of them, so thanks for that. Hope to meet again soon.” Sabir denies rape and conspiracy to rape.

In May 2025 the husband made contact with another stranger on the site, the court heard. Jordan Wallace, 31, a building supplies employee from Wythenshawe in Manchester, said he was “pissed” and asked the husband to pick him up.

He wrote: “13 mins if [you] wanna pick me up [and] me [and] [you] will get perverted with your wife.” When the husband declined to collect him, he said he would ride his bicycle over to the address.

Wallace was “fully aware” the wife was unconscious, and “because of her state of consciousness she was not able to consent to any sexual activity”, Oakley told the court.

She said the husband “recalls that at one point Jordan Wallace ‘got rough’ with [his wife] and he had to actually push him away, saying, ‘What the fuck are you doing?’ telling him he was going to wake her up”.

Wallace later apologised but asked the husband to send the videos he had taken, which he did, the court heard. Wallace has pleaded not guilty to rape and attempted rape.

In June 2025, the husband subjected his wife “to a humiliating, degrading and sustained sexual assault” over the course of three hours, and again invited two men in succession into their home to assault her.

The second man, Alan Keelan, 42, an industrial cleaning firm worker also from Wythenshawe, had climbed on top of the unconscious woman wearing a pair of black women’s knickers and attempted to have sex with her, the court heard.

When he was unable to, he sexually assaulted her before climbing off the bed, the court heard. Keelan denies attempted rape and assault by penetration.

In July last year, the husband again posted on the swingers website, and made contact with the sheet-metal worker Richard Townsend, 38, the court heard. Townsend was aware the woman was not conscious when he proceeded to sexually assault her, assisted by her husband, the jury was told.

The woman’s leg moved, and “it was clear she was restless and stirring, so together they decided enough was enough for that night and he left”, the court heard. Townsend, of Heywood, Greater Manchester, denies assault by penetration.

Jonathan Kirk, 43, from Stockport, was described as “more cautious” than the other defendants, and first requested to meet the husband at his own house.

The husband visited Kirk at his house in August and showed him photographs of the woman passed out and being abused by him. He told Kirk he would consider drugging his wife, and Kirk, a paramedic, told him that “could be very dangerous”, the court heard.

Later, Kirk took a taxi to the husband’s house. “As a senior paramedic, he cannot have failed to notice she was not conscious. He is trained to spot that,” Oakley told the court. “The truth is, he knew and that’s how he wanted her to be.”

After having sexual intercourse with the woman, “Jonathan Kirk stood up and said, ‘fucking hell, wow’ and how great it had been before he left”, the court heard.

Kirk denies rape and conspiracy to rape.

Two other men are also on trial. Robert Stewart, 70, of Stockport, denies rape, conspiracy to rape and conspiracy to administer a substance with intent.

David Graves, 60, of Ilkeston, Derbyshire, denies “non-contact” offences of conspiracy to rape, conspiracy to assault by penetration and conspiracy to administer a substance with intent.

Peers, 38, from Stockport; Brougham, 74, from Cheshire, and another man, Keith Fotheringham, 59, from Dundee, have pleaded guilty to offences against the same woman.

Karl Lindsay, 56, from Somerset has also pleaded guilty to “non-contact” offences. All will be sentenced alongside the husband, at a later date.

The trial continues.
output.standfirst: A jury is hearing how nine men are accused of taking part in, or encouraging online, the sexual abuse of a woman in Stockport, after her husband admitted more than 60 offences against her
output.progress: The case is being heard by a jury at Manchester Minshull Street crown court, with the trial continuing.

output.headline: Fortified plant milk could prevent micronutrient deficiencies, researchers say
output.bodyHtml:
Plant-based alternatives to dairy can avoid causing micronutrient deficiencies if they are fortified, as some brands already do, researchers have found. Without fortification, switching from dairy products to plant-based alternatives could lead to deficiencies in vital micronutrients, especially among young people and women.

Even moving partly to vegan alternatives to milk, cheese and yoghurt could lead to falls in iodine, calcium, riboflavin and vitamin B12 if the substitutes, often based on soya, almonds or oats, are not fortified, scientists said.

The greatest concerns surround iodine, a trace element used by the thyroid gland to produce hormones that regulate metabolism and support healthy growth and brain development. More than half of UK teenage girls already have inadequate iodine intake, the researchers said.

Replacing a fifth to a third of dairy intake with plant-based alternatives would lead to prevalence of iodine deficiency rising from 54% to 65% of adolescent girls and from 32% to 42% of women aged 19 to 49 years old, according to modelling based on typical market levels of fortification.

“There are known health effects of iodine deficiency and that’s why we want to raise awareness of this,” said Dr Sarah Bath, an associate professor in public health nutrition at the University of Surrey. “The population groups that seem to be at risk and have the lowest intakes were the young women and women of childbearing age, and that’s the key life stage where iodine is particularly important.”

Plant-based alternatives to milk, cheese and yoghurt have grown in popularity, though there are signs some consumers are shifting back.

In the UK, children get about half, and adults about a third, of their total iodine intake from dairy products, but there is no formal requirement for vegan alternatives to be fortified with micronutrients.

The researchers looked at the impact of replacing dairy with plant-based alternatives on the UK market, including 146 non-dairy milks, 76 yoghurts and 67 cheeses. While 61% had added calcium and 46% added vitamin B12, only 19% were fortified with riboflavin and 12% with iodine.

At these levels, the scientists’ modelling showed that swapping a third of dairy intake for vegan alternatives led to a 9% to 21% drop in iodine intake, with calcium, riboflavin and vitamin B12 also falling. Switching to 100% non-dairy alternatives led to inadequate levels of iodine reaching 80% in teenage girls and 72% in teenage boys.

Requiring all non-dairy alternatives to be fortified with iodine would prevent average declines, the study found. Adding iodised salt to bread helped reduce the proportion of teenage girls with inadequate iodine intake in the modelled scenarios. The study is published in the Lancet Planetary Health.

Some companies already fortify their dairy substitutes. Niamh Brannelly, the head of nutrition and science communications for Danone in the UK, said its core range of Alpro products was fortified for calcium, iodine and vitamins B2 and B12.

Caroline Orfila Jenkins, a vice-president for science and technology at Oatly, said all its unflavoured, non-organic oat drinks were fortified with nutrients including iodine, calcium, riboflavin and vitamins B12 and D. “This research underlines the importance of appropriate fortification as diets become more plant-based,” she said.

Nichola Ludlam-Raine, a registered dietitian and spokesperson for the British Dietetic Association, said the work raised an important population-level concern but did not mean that everyone who switched would become nutrient-deficient because overall diet mattered too.

“For anyone choosing plant-based milk, I’d recommend checking the label and choosing one fortified with iodine, such as Alpro,” she said. “Organic drinks aren’t fortified with added nutrients, so they’re unlikely to provide iodine. White fish such as cod or haddock, as well as eggs and yoghurt and kefir for those who consume them, can also contribute iodine. I wouldn’t recommend relying on seaweed or kelp supplements as an iodine source, as the iodine content can vary widely and may be excessive.”
output.standfirst: Fortifying plant-based dairy alternatives with iodine and other nutrients would prevent shortfalls, researchers say, after finding unfortified versions could leave young people and women short of key micronutrients
output.progress: Brands including Alpro and Oatly already fortify their plant-based drinks with iodine, calcium and vitamin B12, and dietitians advise choosing these.

output.headline: Milburn review calls for Danish-style ‘flexi-jobs’ guarantee for disabled young people
output.bodyHtml:
The British state should create and subsidise paid jobs for thousands of disabled young people as part of an “opportunity revolution” aimed at reversing years of labour market discrimination, the Milburn review of youth employment will recommend.

The review, due to report this month, will say the government should introduce “flexi-jobs” alongside employment subsidies and intensive skills support to make it easier for disabled and chronically ill 16- to 24-year-olds to get work.

It will argue that the state should step in to underwrite jobs for young people who are locked out of employment and training opportunities, as part of an overhaul of what it sees as an outdated welfare and skills system.

Related: Tell us: are you a young person in northern England struggling to find work?

About a million young people are now classified as “Neet”, meaning they are not in education, employment or training. Nearly half (45%) of those are disabled or in ill health. Disabled young people are three times as likely to be Neet as their non-disabled peers.

The review’s author, the former Labour cabinet minister Alan Milburn, has described soaring numbers of Neets as a moral and economic crisis, warning that failure to tackle rising youth disengagement from work risks creating a “lost generation”.

He has rejected what he has called “myths” about young people being “snowflakes”, insisting that the crisis in youth mental health is real, most youngsters want to work, and it is the duty of government and employers to provide support and opportunities.

The review will say young people with disabilities need a flexible and supportive approach to work that acknowledges fluctuating medical conditions and lack of work experience, and recognises the importance of part-time roles in helping them build confidence.

One eye-catching recommendation is for the UK to adopt a Danish-style “flexi-job” scheme. This guarantees disabled participants employment while allowing them to set working hours – in some cases starting with as few as four hours a week – that suit their individual capacities, with wages topped up by the government.

It will also call for creative ways of shaping jobs to individual capabilities, such as “job carving”: splitting the three component parts of a single entry-level role and matching youngsters to each of those roles. A retail role that comprises stock-filling, till work and locking up would become three job opportunities.

Nearly half of 24-year-old Neets have never worked, and Milburn argued in his interim report earlier this year that abandoning a cohort of Covid-era youngsters coping with high levels of depression, anxiety, autism and ADHD would have a scarring effect on their life chances and lifetime earnings.

Milburn has suggested that the state should switch some of the £4bn a year it spends on disability benefits for young people into comprehensive, high-quality employment and training support, though the government has said it will not endorse “crude cuts” to benefits.

However, he will probably face pushback from campaigners, and potentially backbench Labour MPs, who argue that job support should not be funded by disability benefit cuts that would push many young people into poverty and further away from the job market.

Milburn’s proposals are in part a recognition that young people with disabilities face huge barriers around recruitment processes and inflexible job design, and many businesses are unlikely to create job opportunities for them without government support.

The plans have echoes of the postwar Remploy scheme, which created state-funded workplaces providing “sheltered” employment for disabled ex-service personnel. At its height, Remploy had 90 factories across the UK, the last closing in 2013.

Related: Labour’s pledge to level-up minimum wage for under-20s before next election in doubt

The review will urge large employers to voluntarily adopt employment targets for disabled 16- to 24-year-olds, although it is expected to stop short of recommending statutory quotas.

As well as creating jobs, the review will call for a boost for job support, including supported internships, placements, specialist job matching and coaching, and support for employers to provide workplace adjustments.

Milburn, who has previously called for a “turbo-charging” of specialist internships for young people with special educational needs moving on from school and college, has been critical of the limited ambitions of existing government job support programmes.

The most common conditions reported by disabled Neets were depression, bad nerves or anxiety (23.8%), followed by autism (22.7%) and other health problems or disabilities (18.5%), according to the latest official figures.
output.standfirst: Exclusive: Alan Milburn’s review of youth unemployment will recommend state-backed ‘flexi-jobs’, subsidies and intensive skills support for disabled under-25s, who are three times as likely as their peers to be out of education, employment or training
output.progress: Alan Milburn’s review will call for state-backed flexi-jobs, job carving and employer hiring targets to get disabled young people into work.

output.headline: Ministers consider limits on smart glasses sales and use
output.bodyHtml:
The government is considering placing restrictions on smart glasses amid concerns the technology is being used to surreptitiously film women, a minister has said.

Speaking in the House of Commons, the safeguarding minister, Satvir Kaur, hinted at a ban on selling the technology “to certain users”.

Kaur said: “The benefits of smart glasses must be weighed against the harms they can cause. The government is already looking into options to restrict smart glasses in certain settings and restricting the sale to certain users.”

The minister said people who used smart glasses for filming already risked breaking the law in certain settings, such as in a court where cameras are prohibited.

Kaur added: “Other settings, such as healthcare and education, have existing safeguarding or professional policies that are relevant to smart glasses and any kind of digital recording. NHS England and the Department for Education are currently looking into wearable technology in certain settings as well.”

Anna Sabine, a Liberal Democrat MP and a culture spokesperson for the party who held Wednesday’s debate, said: “Women are reporting waking up after nights out to find videos of themselves have gone viral online, filmed without their knowledge or consent by men wearing smart glasses.

“To me, these devices not only have the potential to erode safety and privacy in public spaces, but raise really important questions about consent.”

Related: The eyes have it: Reform politician’s ‘smart glasses’ prompt calls for ban in Westminster

She said one of the selling points of the glasses in advertisements was that they could be used “to film discreetly”. Sabine said she wanted parliamentarians to act before, rather than after, the harm was done, rather than “only regulate once it is too late”.

Kaur said smart glasses, which can come with built-in cameras, microphones and displays, could “be hugely beneficial” to some people. “For example, for those that are visually impaired, smart glasses have been a gamechanger, helping them navigate the world around them.”

A politician in the Senedd has defended his use of smart glasses in the debating chamber. Jason O’Connell, a Reform UK MS for Pontypridd Cynon Merthyr, read a speech from an in-built teleprompter feature in his glasses last month.

He told the BBC’s Politics Wales: “One of the things I identified, a weakness of mine, was that my head was down looking at my notes a lot and I wanted to get away from that.”
output.standfirst: Safeguarding minister Satvir Kaur says the government is considering restrictions on smart glasses sales and use, after MPs raised cases of women secretly filmed without consent and the footage shared online
output.progress: Ministers are exploring sales restrictions and setting-specific rules, while NHS England and the Department for Education review wearable-tech policy.
